passages.happening:
The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron together. Israel may eat certain land animals: “You may eat any animal that has a split hoof completely divided and that chews the cud” (verse 3).

An animal with only one of the two marks is not to be eaten. The camel, the rock badger and the rabbit chew the cud but have no divided hoof (verses 4-6). “And the pig, though it has a split hoof completely divided, does not chew the cud; it is unclean for you” (verse 7).

“You must not eat their meat or touch their carcasses; they are unclean for you” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The last chapter ended with a task for the priests: to “distinguish between the holy and the common, between the clean and the unclean”, and to teach Israel (10:10-11). Chapters 11 to 15 are the content of that teaching. They go through the parts of daily life where being clean or unclean was at stake: food, childbirth, skin disease, and what flows from the body. Food comes first, because eating is the most constant thing people do.

A new reader should hold on to one thing from the start. Unclean does not mean evil, and it does not mean dirty. An unclean animal is one of God's creatures. It is simply not for Israel's table. And the wording is careful: ‘unclean for you’. The rule is for Israel. Deuteronomy says that a foreigner could eat what an Israelite could not (Deuteronomy 14:21). These laws marked out one people's calling. They were never given as a diet for the whole world.

The two marks are easy to see: a hoof split in two, and chewing the cud, as cattle, sheep and goats do. The chapter sorts animals by what an ordinary person could observe, not by modern biology. The rock badger is the hyrax, a small furry animal of rocky hillsides, and the ‘rabbit’ is most likely the hare. Neither brings up its food to chew it again as a cow does. But both move their jaws all the time as though chewing.

Touching the carcass of such an animal made a person unclean for a time. It was not a sin, and it passed by evening.
passages.later:
The Bible's story of food has a shape. In the beginning God gave plants for food (Genesis 1:29). After the flood he said to Noah, “Everything that lives and moves will be food for you” (Genesis 9:3). At Sinai, Israel's table is made narrower, as a sign of its calling.

Deuteronomy gives a shorter list of the same animals, and begins, “You must not eat any detestable thing” (Deuteronomy 14:3).

In exile in Babylon, keeping these laws became a matter of loyalty: “But Daniel made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king’s food or wine” (Daniel 1:8).
passages.asks: For Israel, every meal was a small act of belonging to God. Ask what daily habit of yours, if any, reminds you whose you are. And ask whether you look down on another believer's practice with food or drink, or let them look down on yours.

passages.happening:
“Of all the creatures that live in the water, whether in the seas or in the streams, you may eat anything with fins and scales” (verse 9). Water creatures without both are ‘detestable’ (verses 10-12).

A list of birds follows that must not be eaten, among them the eagle, the vultures, the kite, the falcon, the raven, the owls, the hawk, the stork and the heron. The list ends with the bat (verses 13-19).

Flying insects are forbidden, with one group left out: those “having jointed legs above their feet for hopping on the ground” (verse 21). “Of these you may eat any kind of locust, katydid, cricket, or grasshopper” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The chapter sorts creatures by the three realms of Genesis 1: land, water and air. The phrase ‘any kind of’ echoes the words of Genesis about creatures made ‘according to their kinds’. The food laws are set inside creation. The animal world is God's ordered world, and Israel's table follows that order.

For fish the rule is plain: fins and scales. For birds no rule is given, only a list. Many of the Hebrew names are uncertain, and translations differ. Most of the birds that can be identified are birds of prey or eaters of dead flesh. The bat is on the list because the Hebrew word covers any creature that flies.

Locusts were food in that world. John the Baptist lived on them in the desert.

A stronger word appears here. Some creatures are called not only unclean but ‘detestable’. A related word is used elsewhere for idols. Israel was to turn away from these foods entirely.

Why these creatures and not others? The chapter gives no reason for any one animal. The note on the last passage sets out the main answers readers have given.
passages.later:
Matthew says of John the Baptist, “His food was locusts and wild honey” (Matthew 3:4). His diet kept this chapter's rule.

Jesus used two creatures from this chapter in a single saying. A gnat is among the smallest unclean things, and a camel is the largest animal named here. He said to some teachers of his day, “You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel” (Matthew 23:24). They were careful in small matters and careless about justice and mercy.

In the story of the lost son, the young man ends up feeding pigs, and longs to eat what they eat (Luke 15:15-16). For Jewish hearers nothing could show more plainly how far from home he had gone.
passages.asks: Jesus warned against straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel. Ask where you are careful about small rules and careless about large ones, such as justice, mercy and faithfulness. And ask what in God's created order you have stopped noticing or respecting.

passages.happening:
“Whoever touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening, and whoever picks up one of their carcasses must wash his clothes, and he will be unclean until evening” (verses 24-25).

Small creatures that move along the ground are named: the mole, the mouse, lizards of several kinds (verses 29-30). If one dies and falls on something made of wood, cloth or leather, the thing is rinsed and is unclean until evening (verse 32). If it falls into a clay pot, the pot must be broken (verse 33).

“Nevertheless, a spring or cistern containing water will remain clean” (verse 36). Dry seed stays clean; wet seed does not (verses 37-38). Even the carcass of an animal that may be eaten makes a person unclean until evening (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
This passage is not about eating. It is about touching dead animals, which nobody in a farming village could avoid. A mouse dies in the storeroom. A lizard falls into a jar.

Look at how mild it is. The person is ‘unclean until evening’. He washes his clothes and waits for sunset. That is all. No offering is asked, and no fault is found. This is the clearest picture in the book of what ordinary uncleanness was: a passing state, not a sin.

The rules about things follow from how people understood uncleanness to move. Clay is porous and soaks up what touches it, so a clay pot is broken. Wood, cloth and leather can be washed. Water was thought to carry uncleanness, so wet seed is affected and dry seed is not.

And there is a kindness in verse 36. A spring or a cistern stays clean even if something dies in it. In a dry land where water was scarce, a rule that spoiled a village's well would have been a disaster.

Most of what makes a person unclean in chapters 11 to 15 has to do with death or the loss of life. Verse 39 fits that pattern. Even a clean animal, once dead, makes the one who touches it unclean. The God who lives in the tent is the living God, and the marks of death are kept back from his house.
passages.later:
The same thought, that death makes unclean, runs through the law: “Whoever touches any dead body will be unclean for seven days” (Numbers 19:11).

The Gospels tell of Jesus touching the dead. He took a dead girl by the hand and said, “Little girl, I say to you, get up” (Mark 5:41). Under the law the unclean made the clean unclean. In the Gospel accounts life passes the other way.
passages.asks: Uncleanness in this passage is ordinary, expected and soon over. Ask whether you carry a sense of being stained that God never laid on you. And ask how you treat the people whose work others shrink from: those who handle the dead, the sick, the waste.

passages.happening:
Creatures that move along the ground are not to be eaten, whether they crawl on the belly or walk on many feet (verses 41-42). “Do not defile yourselves by any crawling creature” (verse 43).

Then the reason. “For I am the LORD your God; consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, because I am holy” (verse 44). “For I am the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt so that I would be your God; therefore be holy, because I am holy” (verse 45).

The chapter closes: “You must distinguish between the unclean and the clean, between animals that may be eaten and those that may not” (verse 47).
passages.hearers:
After forty-three verses of animals, the language suddenly rises. ‘Be holy, because I am holy.’ This is the first time Leviticus uses those words. They will become the motto of the second half of the book.

Holy means set apart for God. The chapter says that Israel's holiness reaches as far as the kitchen table. It is not kept for the sanctuary. It shows in the most ordinary acts of the day.

Verse 45 gives the ground: ‘who brought you up out of the land of Egypt’. The food laws are not a way to earn God's favor. They are part of the life of a people he has already rescued. Later the book says what the laws did: “I have set you apart from the nations to be My own” (20:26). What Israel ate reminded it every day whose people it was. And a people who could not share every table with their neighbors stayed a people.

These laws shaped Jewish history. Around 167 BC the king Antiochus IV tried to stamp out Jewish practice in Judea. The books of Maccabees tell of Jews who were ordered to eat pork and died sooner than do it. Many Jewish families keep these laws today, with love and care, as a way of honoring God in daily life.
passages.later:
Peter repeats verse 44 to Christians, and applies it to the whole of life: “But just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do, for it is written: ‘Be holy, because I am holy’” (1 Peter 1:15-16).

Jesus taught, “Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him” (Mark 7:18), and Mark adds a comment: “(Thus all foods are clean.)” (Mark 7:19).

In Acts, Peter sees a sheet full of animals of every kind and hears, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (Acts 10:15). He gives its meaning himself a few verses later: “God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean” (Acts 10:28).
passages.hard:
Why were these animals unclean, and do Christians have to keep these laws?

The chapter gives no reason for any single animal, and readers have offered several. Some point to health. The medieval Jewish scholar Maimonides held this in part, since pork and shellfish can carry disease. Others answer that clean animals carry disease too, and that the Bible never gives health as the reason. Some think the forbidden animals were tied to the worship of other gods. That fits a few cases and not most. The anthropologist Mary Douglas argued that clean animals are those that fit their realm completely, like fish with fins and scales, while unclean ones blur the lines; the laws taught wholeness and order. Jacob Milgrom stressed reverence for life. Many of the forbidden creatures are hunters or eat dead flesh, and these laws, with the ban on blood, limited the taking of life. The text's own reason is holiness: Israel is to be set apart, because God is.

On Christian practice, most churches follow the New Testament passages quoted above and do not keep the food laws. They hold that the laws were fulfilled in Christ. Did Jesus himself set the food laws aside, or did the church draw that conclusion later? Scholars differ, and the note on Mark 7:14-23 sets out the views. Peter's vision in Acts 10 is first of all about people, with the question of food following from it.

Some Christians do keep these laws. Seventh-day Adventists avoid the meats this chapter calls unclean. Many Jewish believers in Jesus keep the food laws as part of their Jewish life. Paul asked believers on each side not to judge the other: “The one who eats everything must not belittle the one who does not, and the one who does not eat everything must not judge the one who does, for God has accepted him” (Romans 14:3).

None of this treats the food laws as foolish. God gave them, and they did their work. Jewish families who keep them today are honoring the God of Abraham.
passages.asks: God's reason for the food laws was himself: be holy, because I am holy. Ask what it would mean for holiness to reach your own kitchen table, your shopping, your eating and drinking. And ask whether your idea of holiness is mostly about what you avoid, or about whom you belong to.
